newsitem.title: USA: Pentagon expands Gulf War illness team.
newsitem.headline: Pentagon expands Gulf War illness team.

text.p: Under growing pressure from Gulf War veterans, the Pentagon said on Tuesday it was increasing from 12 to 110 the number of people investigating the causes of "Persian Gulf Illness."
Deputy Defence Secretary John White announced the move at a Pentagon news conference and named Assistant Navy Secretary Bernard Rostker to head the expanded effort.

The Pentagon has denied any cover-up of possible exposure of U.S. troops to Iraqi chemical weapons in the 1991 Gulf War, saying there is no evidence of U.S. deaths or injuries from chemical agents or of Iraqi use of them against U.S. forces.

But it said on Oct. 20 it was notifying about 20,000 U.S. Gulf War veterans that they might have been exposed to chemical weapons when American troops destroyed the Kamisiyah weapons dump in southern Iraq in March 1991.
Pressure has been growing for years from Gulf War veterans groups for the Pentagon to find the cause of unexplained complaints among thousands of former troops ranging from numbness to memory loss.
"It has become apparent that there is still much that is unknown about how Gulf War service may have affected the health of those who served," White said in a statement.

"New information recently gathered from a variety of sources, including individuals who served, demands new and different expertise. For this reason it is important to ensure this new organisation has the proper priority and sufficient resources to ensure we are taking the best possible care of those who served."

The Pentagon has said it has found no common cause of widespread complaints from Gulf War veterans. But President Bill Clinton, honouring U.S. veterans on Monday, said his administration was making every effort to learn why many of them had developed unexplained illnesses.

"I want to assure all of you that we will leave no stone unturned in our efforts to investigate these cases and to provide our Gulf War veterans with the medical care they need," he told a large crowd at the Tomb of the Unknowns.
He said the presidential advisory commission he had appointed to respond to the health concerns of Gulf veterans would hand in its report by the end of the year.

The Washington Post last week said the panel's preliminary report had found no evidence that chemical weapons had caused the illnesses of Gulf veterans but said a final decision would have to wait until more than 100 studies by government and civilian researchers were completed.
